scenes.caption: "You were unprofessional" is an opinion. "You interrupted twice" is something a person can fix.
Name the Situation (when and where), the Behavior (what anyone could see or hear) and the Impact (what it did).
Because you describe rather than label, the other person has less to defend and more to work with.
Then stop talking and listen to their side.
The default rewards for great work are praise and extra volume. Neither helps high performers grow.
A stretch: a harder problem with real ownership, slightly beyond what they have done, with you available but not hovering.
Illustrative: thirty more tickets is only load. Owning the new-joiner escalation guide, reviewed in six weeks, is a stretch.
Ask where they want to be in a year, then find work that gets them closer.
Same mistake, third time. Before you call it a performance problem, check what the system is rewarding.
Ask in order: Do they know the standard? Can they do it, given skill, tools and time? Does anything reward the mistake?
Illustrative: the queue is heavy and closures count towards the daily target. Check what that is rewarding first.
Only if all three are fine is it a willingness problem, and that needs a direct, documented conversation.
Managers usually see closed tickets, not the mentoring, ad-hoc questions, rework and meetings that eat capacity.
For one week, each person jots down how half-days split between these four. Bars are illustrative, not data.
Compare it to what you assumed. The gap shows where load is real and who may be overcommitted.
Do not use it to police anyone. Tell people how you will use it before they begin.
The WHO's ICD-11 names three dimensions of burn-out: exhaustion, growing mental distance or cynicism, and reduced effectiveness.
It is not a medical diagnosis, and managers are not clinicians.
Your role: notice changes against a person's own baseline, ask openly, and adjust the work.
On the self-check, two or more yeses is a reason for a kind, private conversation, not a conclusion.
Researchers separate task conflict (ideas, methods, priorities) from relationship conflict (friction between people).
Early work suggested task conflict could help. A later meta-analysis found both types linked to worse performance.
The two were strongly linked: arguments about work easily turn personal. Effects appear to depend on context.
Before a contested decision, agree the criteria first, then argue about options against them.
Every time you answer a question instantly, you teach them to keep asking.
Coaching swaps the answer for a question: What have you tried? What are your options? What would you do if I were away?
GROW is a common structure for coaching conversations: Goal, Reality, Options, Will.
Coaching is not interrogation: if they lack knowledge or it is urgent, just tell them.
In investing, loss aversion means a loss weighs more than an equal gain. How large the effect is remains debated.
Change triggers the same asymmetry: people weigh what they stand to lose, such as expert status, routines and certainty.
Resistance may be rational accounting, not stubbornness. Applying this to change is an interpretation, not a tested result.
A good adviser names the losses, shrinks them and makes the gains concrete and near-term.
"Disagree and commit" is not permission to stop arguing; it is an obligation to argue first.
Amazon's principle: challenge a decision you disagree with, even when uncomfortable, then fully commit once it is made.
Used well, it prevents endless consensus-seeking. Used badly, it ends debate before it has started.
Illustrative: argue your case with data. If the decision stands, present it as your own and track the problems you predicted.
Orders say what to do; commander's intent says why: the purpose of the operation and the end state wanted.
When circumstances change and the plan stops making sense, people who know the intent can adapt without new instructions.
Facing ambiguity, give purpose, desired end state and constraints, and leave the method open.
Add "The intent is..." to your next briefing, then ask someone to repeat it back in their own words.
"Management decided" is the sentence that costs a leader the most trust. Say it as your own, not as a message from above.
State the decision, explain the reasons, say what was rejected, separate fixed from open, and describe what happens next.
Then allow time for reaction before moving to the plan.
Saying yes to every request feels helpful until the commitments start to collide. (Schematic.)
A boundary is not a refusal of the person; it is a clear statement of what you can do and when.
A useful shape: "I can do X by Friday, or Y next week, but not both. Which matters more?"
Illustrative: offer a basic report tomorrow or a complete one on Monday, and say month-end work would slip. They choose Monday.
The fastest explanation is a person. Deming argued that most failures come from the system managers control.
If a competent, well-meaning person could make the same error, blaming one person fixes nothing; the next one repeats it.
Instead, remove the trap, add a check, or make the right action easier.
Personal accountability remains for deliberate or repeated disregard.
In a 1974 paper, Tversky and Kahneman spun a wheel of fortune rigged to stop at 10 or 65.
Participants said whether the share of African countries in the UN was higher or lower than that number, then estimated it.
Median estimates: about 25% for the group that saw 10, and about 45% for the group that saw 65.
The first number shapes the answers that follow. Write your own estimate privately before hearing anyone else's.
People judged which of three lines matched a standard line, an easy task. Lines here are schematic.
But the rest of the group, actually confederates, unanimously gave a wrong answer on certain trials.
A substantial share went along at least once, though most answers were still correct. Later rates vary by culture and era.
When even one other person disagreed with the majority, conformity dropped sharply.
Norton, Mochon and Ariely (2012): people valued things they assembled themselves more than identical ones built by others.
Effort and a sense of ownership raise the value we assign, and the effect weakens if the project is not completed.
Illustrative: a team rates its in-house tracker above a cheaper off-the-shelf tool that does the same job.
Scoring both against the same criteria, written down in advance, gives a fairer comparison.
The idea: self-control draws on a limited resource, so using it once leaves less for the next task. (Schematic.)
Baumeister and colleagues (1998) reported that people who resisted chocolate gave up sooner on a later puzzle. It was widely taught.
A 2016 multi-lab replication by Hagger and colleagues, across 23 labs, found an effect close to zero. Bars are schematic.
The idea is now contested; some researchers defend modified versions. Ask whether a large replication confirmed it.
We explain our own mistakes by the situation and other people's by their character.
Observers tend to overweight personality and underweight the situation, which Lee Ross named the fundamental attribution error.
Illustrative: an agent with low CSAT is called uncaring. Review shows he was given the escalated cases others avoided.
The bias varies across cultures and contexts. Before judging, name two situational explanations and check one.
Elizabeth Newton (1990) asked people to tap out well-known songs for listeners to guess, as reported in Made to Stick.
Tappers predicted listeners would guess about half the songs; listeners guessed very few. Check the original before quoting.
The tapper hears the melody and cannot un-hear it. Camerer, Loewenstein and Weber named this the curse of knowledge in 1989.
Illustrative: "Just check the VDR logs for the usual pattern." The new agent nods, then guesses.
Fisher and Ury separate positions, what people say they want, from interests, why they want it.
Bargaining over positions tends to produce deadlock or a split down the middle.
Illustrative: she insists on the day shift. Asking why reveals 4 pm school pickups. A shift starting at 7 am solves it.
Many conflicts are incompatible positions on top of compatible interests. Ask: "What would that give you?"
